summary.title: Memory Allocation
summary.one_liner: A visual, interactive walkthrough of how memory allocators handle malloc and free, from simple free lists to fragmentation, slab allocators and boundary-tag bookkeeping.
takeaways: A simple allocator can track free and allocated blocks in lists; malloc searches the free list and free returns blocks to it.
Fragmentation happens when free memory is split into small pieces that cannot satisfy a larger request; coalescing adjacent free blocks helps.
Over-allocating or segmenting memory by size class (slab allocators) reduces fragmentation but costs wasted space.
Boundary tag allocators store size and state bookkeeping in-line next to each block so adjacent free blocks can be merged quickly.
Allocators rely on program correctness; magic values can help detect buffer overruns and use-after-free bugs, usually enabled only when debugging.
summary.summary: The article uses small visualisations to explain what a memory allocator does when a program calls malloc and free. It starts with a trivial bump-style allocator, then builds a general-purpose free-list allocator and shows how coalescing adjacent free blocks reduces fragmentation. It then covers over-allocation and size-segregated slab allocators as trade-offs, the malloc(0) edge case, and in-line bookkeeping (boundary tags) that allows coalescing. Examples are in JavaScript, with one short C snippet, and it links to an interactive playground for writing your own allocator.
